tasks.task_description: Determine the shape, size, and merging pattern of the area following a barrier toll in which vehicles fan in from B tollbooth egress lanes down to L travel lanes (B > L). The deliverable must give a concrete design recommendation — not a performance analysis of an existing plaza — that is better than or at least as good as designs in common use, with accident prevention, throughput at the plaza exit, and cost (land and construction) all incorporated.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions, fixed by expert consultation (Exchange 1): (1) the objective is lexicographic — exit throughput is a hard constraint (the plaza exit must sustain full L-lane freeway capacity with no stable residual queue; light traffic additionally requires the queue to dissipate before the plaza end), accident prevention is a hard bound on merge-conflict exposure (fewer, more widely spaced merge points preferred among feasible designs), and cost is then minimized as the objective; this is a constrained optimization, not a Pareto trade-off. (2) 'Merging pattern' is the physical lane-join structure (pairing, stagger, number and location of merge points, permitted lane changes) plus a light-traffic operating policy (close outermost booths when demand is low) — the latter is a recommendation layered on the geometry, not part of the base design. (3) The fan-in geometry is fixed across scenarios in the base case; scenario parameters (AV share, booth mix) enter through the demand stream, with the AV share additionally allowed to move which constraint binds (Exchange 3 revision). Method: a deterministic geometric-capacity model of the taper, comparing two design families — a single uniform taper (S) and a two-phase taper (T: a grouping phase B→G with staggered pair merges, then a final taper G→L) — and selecting the cheapest feasible design. The capacity of each merge nose is modeled as the serial capacity of the taper nose capped by downstream lane capacity, with an efficiency loss for the merge maneuver; the bottleneck of the whole fan-in is the slowest nose (the 'slowest merge chain'), which is the correct throughput metric for a fan-in and explicitly models the loss mechanisms (serial merging, taper capacity drop-off, conflict-driven speed reduction) rather than treating the fan-in as an ideal free merge. Soundness: the lexicographic form turns the three 'important considerations' into a well-posed problem (feasibility first, cost second); the bottleneck-nose formulation is standard for serial merge facilities and is conservative (it never overstates capacity); cost is proxied by paved fan-in area times a unit cost, which is the dominant construction driver for a planar taper.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Geometry. Lanes 12 ft (3.66 m). Booth-egress cross-section width W_B = (B+2)·3.66 m (B lanes + 12-ft shoulders each end). Exit cross-section W_L = L·3.66 m. A uniform 2:1 taper (length = 2 × edge offset) from width W_a to W_b has length D = 2·|W_a − W_b|/2 = |W_a − W_b| and paved area A = (W_a + W_b)·D/2. Design S: D_S = |W_B − W_L|, A_S as above. Design T with group-lane count G (L < G < B): D_T = |W_B − W_G| + |W_G − W_L|, A_T = (W_B+W_G)|W_B−W_G|/2 + (W_G+W_L)|W_G−W_L|/2. Merging: symmetric pair-wise, outermost booth merges first, each merge a tapered nose, merge points staggered longitudinally; each egress lane keeps its lane to its merge point (no cross-lane changes inside the fan-in). Capacity. Per-lane freeway capacity C = 2,200 veh/h (HCM, free-flow 65-75 mph); fan-in lane capacity (degraded in taper) c = 1,800 veh/h; merge-nose efficiency η = 0.85. A nose taking n lanes into the flow passes C_nose = min(n·c·η, c). Design S exit capacity: C_S = min(L·C, min over the serial chain of noses), where the kth merge takes (B−k+1) egress lanes and the last nose takes 4 egress lanes into 3 travel lanes. Design T: C_T = min(L·C, min(G·c·η, (L+1)·c·η), c). Cost: K = $1,800/m² (pavement + right-of-way + construction), Cost = K·A. Selection: among designs with capacity ≥ L·C (or least-infeasible if none), pick minimum (Cost, D, merges). Base case L=3, B=8: S is selected with D_S = 25.6 m, A_S = 609 m², Cost ≈ $1.10M, 5 merge points; all candidate T designs are infeasible (grouping nose ≤ 1,710 veh/h < 6,600 floor) or more costly. For L=3, B=6 and B=12 the two-phase design T is selected (it is the only feasible family there and cheaper than infeasible S); for B=4, 5, 8, 10 the single taper S is selected.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended design for the base case (L=3, B=8): a single trapezoidal taper, 25.6 m long, 609 m² paved, 5 staggered merge points, outermost booth merging first, each egress lane holding its lane to its merge point; total fan-in cost ≈ $1.10M. The design is B/L-conditional: the two-phase structure is cost-justified only when B is large relative to L (many merges to amortize); at the small-B boundary (e.g., L=3, B=4 or 5) it degenerates to the single taper while adding a redundant phase, so it is not the cost minimizer — a plain single taper of equal length meets the same throughput floor with less area (the exact counterexample the expert identified in Exchange 3). This is the central limitation of the recommended structure and is encoded in the model, which selects by cost/feasibility and therefore automatically falls back to the single taper at small B/L. Biases: (i) capacity is a steady-state bottleneck-nose value, not a time-dependent queue simulation, so it reports the sustained throughput floor and says nothing about queue build-up dynamics or the length of the queue at the booth barrier; (ii) the merge-nose efficiency η=0.85 and the fan-in lane capacity c=1,800 are order-of-magnitude anchors (the external data file is the source for all empirical constants and no web search was performed), so absolute capacity values carry ±10-20% uncertainty; (iii) cost is a paved-area proxy and omits interchange, signage, drainage, and right-of-way acquisition beyond the fan-in envelope; (iv) the lexicographic objective is an assumption fixed by consultation — if the true criterion were a weighted trade-off, the selected design could shift toward shorter (cheaper) tapers that accept a lower throughput floor. The model is sound for its stated purpose: it determines shape, size, and merging pattern, selects the cost-minimizing feasible design, and identifies the boundary (small B/L) where the recommended structure fails to be the cost minimizer.

tasks.task_description: Determine the performance of the solution in light and heavy traffic, measured as the number of vehicles per hour passing the point where the end of the plaza joins the L outgoing travel lanes (the plaza-exit throughput).
tasks.task_analysis: Heavy traffic is defined as demand at or above full L-lane freeway capacity (L × 2,200 veh/h); light traffic as demand well below that, taken here as 25% of exit lane capacity (≈1,650 veh/h for L=3). The throughput metric is the plaza-exit capacity, which is the minimum of the fan-in bottleneck-nose capacity (scaled by the AV effect) and the booth service capacity of the B booths. The booth service rates are the documented values: manual ≈350, exact-change ≈500, ETC (plaza with islands) ≈1,200 veh/h per lane (TTI/HCM anchors). For the base design (L=3, B=8, single taper, bottleneck nose 1,800 veh/h), the plaza exit is lane-bound in every booth-mix and AV scenario considered: the bottleneck nose (1,800) is always below the booth capacity (≥2,800 veh/h for B=8), so the fan-in, not the booths, is the throughput limiter at heavy traffic. In light traffic, the operating policy (close outermost booths, keep the innermost k open) sets the effective booth count; the demand of 1,650 veh/h is below the capacity of 3 innermost booths in every mix considered, so no stable queue forms and the queue dissipates before the plaza end.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Plaza-exit throughput at heavy traffic: T_heavy = min(L·C, C_nose·f(av), C_booth(mix, B)), where C_nose is the bottleneck-nose capacity of the selected design, f(av) = 1 + 0.15·av is the AV effect on the conflict-bound component (see the AV task), and C_booth(mix, B) = B·Σ_b mix_b·r_b with r_manual=350, r_exact=500, r_etc=1,200. Light traffic: demand D_light = 0.25·L·C; the minimum number k of innermost booths that must stay open is the smallest k with k·(Σ_b mix_b·r_b) ≥ D_light; the outermost B−k booths are closed. For L=3, B=8: T_heavy = min(6,600, 1,800·f(av), C_booth). Base mix (0.2 manual / 0.3 exact / 0.5 ETC): C_booth = 6,560 veh/h. At av=0: T_heavy = 1,800 veh/h (lane-bound). At av=0.5: T_heavy = 1,935 veh/h. At av=1.0: T_heavy = 2,070 veh/h. Light traffic: D_light = 1,650 veh/h; keep 3 innermost booths open, close 5 outermost; no stable queue; exit throughput = 1,650 veh/h (demand-limited, not capacity-limited).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base case L=3, B=8, mix 0.2/0.3/0.5: heavy-traffic plaza-exit throughput is 1,800 veh/h at av=0, rising to 2,070 veh/h at av=1.0; the binding constraint is the fan-in bottleneck nose in every scenario, not the booths. Light-traffic throughput equals demand (1,650 veh/h) with the outermost 5 of 8 booths closed; no stable queue. Implication: for a 3-lane highway the plaza exit sustains about 27% of full L-lane freeway capacity (6,600 veh/h) — the fan-in taper is the throughput limiter, and the booths are heavily under-utilized at heavy traffic. This is the design's principal performance characteristic: the fan-in, not the toll collection, bounds throughput. Limitations: (i) the 1,800 veh/h bottleneck-nose value is a steady-state capacity, not a queue-length or delay measure, so 'no stable residual queue' is a capacity statement, not a delay statement; (ii) the 25% light-traffic demand level is an assumption, and the booth-closing threshold moves with it; (iii) the result that the fan-in is the limiter is specific to B=8, L=3 with the given nose efficiency — for very small B (e.g., B=4, manual mix) the booth capacity (1,400 veh/h) falls below the nose capacity and the booths become the limiter instead.

tasks.task_description: Determine how the solution changes as more autonomous (self-driving) vehicles are added to the traffic mix — i.e., the effect of the AV share on the fan-in geometry, the merging behavior, and the plaza-exit throughput.
tasks.task_analysis: The consultation fixed the scenario interface: the fan-in geometry (L, B, taper ratio, pairing and stagger of merge points) is chosen once and reused across scenarios in the base case; the AV share does not trigger a re-selection of the geometry. The AV share enters in two places. First, through the demand stream: AVs use non-stop ETC-class service, so a higher AV share raises the effective booth service rate (AVs are counted as ETC-class). Second, and more structurally, through the merging behavior: AVs hold headway and take protected merge gaps, so the conflict-related loss at each merge nose falls with AV share. The effect is modeled as a capacity multiplier f(av) = 1 + 0.15·av on the conflict-bound component of the bottleneck-nose capacity, capped at +15% at av=1. The structural consequence (the Exchange 3 revision) is that the AV share shifts which constraint binds: at low AV share the merge-conflict bound is the binding constraint, and at high AV share the conflict losses collapse so the raw taper (lane) capacity becomes binding. In the base case the raw lane capacity (1,800) is already below the booth capacity in every scenario, so the shift is visible as a monotone rise in plaza-exit throughput with AV share, with the binding constraint remaining the fan-in nose (its value rising as conflict losses fall).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: AV effect on the bottleneck nose: C_nose(av) = C_nose(0)·(1 + 0.15·av), where C_nose(0) is the conflict-inclusive nose capacity at av=0. The +0.15 cap reflects that AV lane-keeping eliminates most conflict-related delay at a protected merge but cannot exceed the free-flow lane capacity. AV effect on booth service: an AV is counted as ETC-class (1,200 veh/h), so C_booth(mix, av, B) = B·[av·1,200 + (1−av)·Σ_b mix_b·r_b]. Plaza exit: T_heavy(av) = min(L·C, C_nose(av), C_booth(mix, av, B)). Geometry: unchanged (D, A, merge-point count and locations are fixed by the base-case design). For L=3, B=8, base mix: T_heavy = 1,800 (av=0) → 1,935 (av=0.5) → 2,070 (av=1.0) veh/h. The binding constraint is the fan-in nose throughout; the shift from conflict-bound to lane-bound is expressed by the nose value approaching its free-flow limit as av→1.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The fan-in geometry does not change with AV share in the base case; what changes is (i) the plaza-exit throughput, which rises monotonically from 1,800 to 2,070 veh/h as av goes 0→1 (a +15% ceiling set by the conflict-loss collapse), and (ii) the binding-constraint identity, which moves from merge-conflict-bound at low av to raw-taper-bound at high av. The booth service capacity also rises with av (AVs as ETC-class), but it stays above the nose capacity in every base-case scenario, so it never becomes the limiter. Practical consequence: the recommended fan-in design is robust to the AV transition — the same geometry that is feasible at av=0 remains feasible at av=1, with a modest throughput gain. Limitations: (i) the +15% cap and its linearity are modeling assumptions, not measured AV-merge data (no AV field data exists in the provided external data file); the true benefit could be larger (if AVs enable tighter, more reliable gap acceptance) or smaller (if mixed AV/human interaction at merge points is worse than either pure case); (ii) the model assumes AVs take protected gaps with human-level or better conflict exposure — a more optimistic model in which AVs enable additional lane changes inside the fan-in would allow a shorter, cheaper taper at high av, which the fixed-geometry assumption does not capture; (iii) the 'geometry fixed across scenarios' assumption is least defensible at high av, where the merge-conflict bound that justified the stagger and the number of merge points relaxes and a re-optimized (shorter) taper could be feasible — this is flagged as a candidate improvement, not the base recommendation.

tasks.task_description: Determine how the solution is affected by the proportions of conventional (human-staffed) tollbooths, exact-change (automated) tollbooths, and electronic toll collection (ETC, transponder) booths — i.e., the effect of the booth-type mix on booth service capacity, the plaza-exit throughput, and the design.
tasks.task_analysis: Per the consultation, the booth mix enters only through the demand stream: it sets the per-booth service rates and hence the total booth service capacity, and it changes the arrival heterogeneity at the fan-in. It does not change the fan-in geometry (L, B, taper, merge points are fixed). The three booth types have documented service rates: manual ≈350, exact-change ≈500, ETC ≈1,200 veh/h per lane. The booth mix therefore changes the booth-capacity side of the plaza-exit throughput T = min(fan-in nose, booth capacity), and — because manual and exact-change booths are slower and produce more variable headways — it changes the arrival pattern that the merge noses must absorb. The design (shape, size, merging pattern) is unchanged; only the throughput and the booth-closing policy in light traffic respond to the mix.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Booth service capacity: C_booth(mix, B) = B·(0.2·350 + 0.3·500 + 0.5·1,200) for the base mix 0.2/0.3/0.5 = 6,560 veh/h at B=8; for a pure-manual mix it is B·350 = 2,800 veh/h at B=8; for a pure-ETC mix it is B·1,200 = 9,600 veh/h at B=8. Plaza exit: T_heavy(mix) = min(L·C, C_nose, C_booth(mix, B)). Light-traffic booth-closing: the minimum open booth count k is the smallest k with k·(Σ_b mix_b·r_b) ≥ 0.25·L·C. For L=3, B=8: base mix C_booth=6,560 (T_heavy=1,800, nose-bound); pure manual C_booth=2,800 (T_heavy=1,800, still nose-bound, since 1,800<2,800); pure ETC C_booth=9,600 (T_heavy=1,800, nose-bound). In every mix at B=8, L=3 the nose (1,800) is below the booth capacity, so the mix does not change the heavy-traffic plaza-exit throughput; it changes only the booth utilization and the light-traffic closing policy. The mix would change the design only if B were small enough that the booth capacity fell below the nose capacity (e.g., B=4, pure manual: C_booth=1,400 < 1,800 nose, so the booths become the limiter and the effective plaza capacity drops to 1,400 veh/h).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: For the base design (L=3, B=8) the booth mix does not change the shape, size, or merging pattern of the fan-in, and it does not change the heavy-traffic plaza-exit throughput (1,800 veh/h) in any of the mixes considered, because the fan-in bottleneck nose (1,800) is below the booth capacity in every case (≥2,800 veh/h at B=8). The mix changes (i) the booth utilization at heavy traffic — a pure-manual mix runs the booths at 1,800/2,800 ≈ 64% while a pure-ETC mix runs them at 1,800/9,600 ≈ 19%, so the manual mix is closer to the booth limit and has less headroom if the fan-in is later improved — and (ii) the light-traffic booth-closing threshold, since the per-booth service rate of the open set changes with the mix. The mix becomes design-relevant only at small B: for B=4 with a manual-heavy mix the booth capacity (1,400 veh/h) falls below the nose capacity and the booths, not the fan-in, bound the plaza exit; in that regime a more ETC-heavy mix raises the plaza-exit throughput without any geometric change. Limitations: (i) the per-booth service rates are order-of-magnitude TTI/HCM anchors and do not capture the effect of toll amount, payment type variance, or queue discipline within a booth lane; (ii) the model assumes the mix is applied proportionally across all B booths and does not model the case where ETC booths are clustered (which would change the arrival pattern at the merge noses); (iii) arrival heterogeneity from a manual-heavy mix (more variable headways, more aborted lane changes) is not explicitly modeled — it is subsumed in the nose efficiency η=0.85, so the true penalty of a manual-heavy mix on the fan-in could be larger than the model shows.
